content: 1. Huang et al. (2020) investigated the use of isoniazid preventive therapy in individuals who were in contact with patients suffering from multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Their findings were published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine. 2. Apolisi et al. (2023) explored tuberculosis diagnosis and the use of preventive monotherapy among children and adolescents exposed to rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis within household settings. This study was detailed in Open Forum Infectious Diseases. 3. Garcia-Prats et al. (2018) assessed the clinical and cardiac safety of long-term levofloxacin use in children undergoing treatment for MDR-TB. Their research was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 4. Malik et al. (2020) evaluated the feasibility and safety of community-based delivery of fluoroquinolone-containing preventive regimens for individuals exposed to drug-resistant tuberculosis. The study appeared in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 5. Malik et al. (2021) examined the effectiveness of preventive therapy for individuals exposed to drug-resistant tuberculosis within households in Karachi, Pakistan. Their findings were published in Emerging Infectious Diseases. 6. Ali et al. (2023) reported on QT interval prolongation associated with the use of one or more QT-prolonging agents as part of a multidrug regimen for rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis treatment. This study was published in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy. 7. Jin et al. (2023) investigated the impact of anti-tuberculosis drug pharmacokinetics on QTc prolongation. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Antimicrobial Agents. 8. Garcia-Prats et al. (2019) studied the pharmacokinetics, safety, and dosing of novel pediatric levofloxacin dispersible tablets in children exposed to MDR-TB. This research was published in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy. 9. Rouzier et al. (2022) explored caregiver willingness to administer tuberculosis preventive therapy (TPT) to children living with drug-resistant TB patients. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease. 10. Suryavanshi et al. (2020) conducted an international, multisite cross-sectional study to assess the willingness of adults and adolescents in household contact with MDR-TB index cases to take preventive therapy. The study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 11. Purchase et al. (2019) evaluated the acceptability of a novel levofloxacin dispersible tablet formulation for young children exposed to MDR-TB. Their findings were published in the Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal. 12. Wademan et al. (2022) examined the practical and psychosocial challenges faced by caregivers that influence the acceptability of MDR-TB preventive therapy for young children. This study was published in PLOS One. 13. Dodd et al. (2022) conducted a modeling study to assess the global impact of household contact management for children on MDR-TB and rifampicin-resistant TB cases, deaths, and health system costs in 2019. Their findings were published in The Lancet Global Health. 14. A qualitative study was conducted to assess the values, preferences, acceptability, and feasibility of levofloxacin (Lfx) as TPT for adult household contacts of MDR-TB patients in five lowand middle-income countries: Georgia, India, Indonesia, South Africa, and Vietnam. Eligible participants were household contacts of newly diagnosed MDR-TB patients, and interviews were conducted to understand their attitudes and perspectives on the use of fluoroquinolones for TPT. 15. A survey was conducted to explore the programmatic feasibility of using levofloxacin for TPT among MDR-TB contacts in anticipation of a WHO recommendation. National TB program managers from 30 high-burden MDR-TB countries were contacted, and 18 responded. The survey assessed current practices, affordability, feasibility, and acceptability of Lfx-based TPT. 16. Most national TB program managers expressed willingness to implement a six-month levofloxacin regimen for MDR-TB contacts following a strong WHO recommendation. The regimen was considered generally affordable and feasible, with potential to increase equity and acceptability among healthcare workers and patients. However, concerns were raised about funding constraints, resource availability, potential resistance to levofloxacin, and increased out-of-pocket expenses for patients.
